newsitem.title: USA: Japan PM - Tokyo trade surplus with U.S. to decline.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM - Tokyo trade surplus with U.S. to decline.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday assured the United States that Tokyo's trade surplus with Washington is likely to fall over the long term.

In a speech prepared for delivery to the National Press Club in Washington, Hashimoto said Japan's planned reforms in six areas including financial, fiscal, and economic systems will help solve many of the individual economic problems between the two countries.

Dissatisfied with slow growth in sales of American goods and services in Japan, Washington has been calling for progress in bilateral negotiations over such issues as automobiles, airline service, shipyards and telecommunications.
In his speech, Hashimoto said Japanese carmakers have made $12 billion worth of investment in the United States to produce cars, part of which are now exported to Europe and Japan.
"Such changes in Japan's economic structures are having a good effect on Japan-U.S. economic relations, and Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. is likely to fall over the long term," he said.

Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. rose 11.2 percent to $3.04 billion in March, the sixth consecutive month in which it had risen year-on-year. The weak Japanese yen against the dollar has helped make the nation's exports more competitive in the U.S. market.
U.S. officials have publicly voiced concern about a resurgence of Tokyo's trade surplus and warned that the rise could threaten renewed trade tension.

Hashimoto said Japan needs to reform its systems and business practices, long the backbone of Tokyo's economic development. "On the contrary, those systems and practices are now preventing further economic development of Japan."

In an apparent attempt to appease U.S. pressure for increased fiscal spending by Japan to prop up the economy, Hashimoto explained that Japan's state budgetary condition is the worst among major industrial nations.
He said the nation's debt in terms of the outstanding value of government bonds totals more than $2 trillion.

Some U.S. officials are worried about Tokyo's plan to sharply tighten budget policy, fearing that the April 1 increase in consumption taxes will slow down economic growth, and thus force Japanese firms to look abroad for sales.
